Lecture 40

Spherical separation and Legendre functions

We separate Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates and prove that Legendre’s equation has a nonzero solution bounded on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) exactly when λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) with an integer ℓ≥0\ell\ge0ℓ≥0. We derive Rodrigues’ formula and the norms of the Legendre polynomials, prove their completeness from polynomial approximation, and expand an axisymmetric potential inside and outside a sphere.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Separate Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates and select the radial powers admissible inside and outside a sphere.
  • Prove that boundedness at x=±1x=\pm1x=±1 forces λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) and a polynomial solution, and check the boundary form at the singular ends.
  • Use Rodrigues’ formula to compute Legendre polynomials, their norms and the coefficients of an expansion.
  • Construct the axisymmetric potential of a sphere with piecewise continuous boundary values and state in which sense it takes them.

Lecture 39 separated the Laplacian in a disc and found a radial problem with one singular endpoint. A sphere leads, after separation in spherical coordinates, to Legendre’s equation on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1), whose coefficient p(x)=1−x2p(x)=1-x^2p(x)=1−x2 vanishes at both ends. In this lecture we decide which solutions are admissible there, construct the Legendre polynomials, prove that they are complete, and use them to find the potential inside and outside a sphere with given boundary values. The lecture reads in three stages: separation and the singular angular problem (Sections 40.1 and 40.2), the Legendre polynomials and their completeness (Sections 40.3 and 40.4), and potentials of a sphere (Section 40.5).

40.2 Bounded solutions and integer modes

We consider real λ\lambdaλ, the values that a separation of real fields produces.

Definition 40.1 (Legendre’s eigenvalue problem). A real number λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of Legendre’s problem if (40.2) has a solution y∈C2(−1,1)y\in C^2(-1,1)y∈C2(−1,1), not identically zero, that is bounded on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1). Such a yyy is an eigenfunction for λ\lambdaλ.

The point 000 is an ordinary point of (40.2). Theorem 40.2 (Eigenvalues of Legendre’s problem). For Legendre’s problem the following hold.

  • Integer modes. The eigenvalues of Legendre’s problem are the numbers λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) with ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}.

  • Polynomial eigenfunctions. For λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) the eigenfunctions are the nonzero multiples of one polynomial of degree ℓ\ellℓ, which is even or odd as ℓ\ellℓ is. So every eigenvalue is simple.

  • Orthogonality. Eigenfunctions yyy and zzz for different eigenvalues satisfy ∫−11y(x)z(x) ⁣dx=0\int_{-1}^1y(x)z(x)\dd x=0∫−11​y(x)z(x)dx=0.

40.3 Legendre polynomials

We now find the polynomial solutions explicitly.

Then the ℓ\ellℓ-th derivative v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)}v(ℓ) is a polynomial of degree ℓ\ellℓ that solves (40.2) with λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1), and v(ℓ)(1)=2ℓℓ!v^{(\ell)}(1)=2^\ell\ell!v(ℓ)(1)=2ℓℓ!.

Summary

Separating Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates gives the radial powers rℓr^\ellrℓ and r−ℓ−1r^{-\ell-1}r−ℓ−1 and, for axisymmetric fields, Legendre’s equation −((1−x2)y′)′=λy-((1-x^2)y')'=\lambda y−((1−x2)y′)′=λy with x=cos⁡θx=\cos\thetax=cosθ. Both ends x=±1x=\pm1x=±1 are singular. Boundedness there forces λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1) and selects the polynomial solution PℓP_\ellPℓ​. For two polynomial solutions the end terms of the boundary form tend to 000. For an unbounded solution they need not, and orthogonality can fail: ∫−11xartanh⁡x ⁣dx=1\int_{-1}^1x\operatorname{artanh}x\dd x=1∫−11​xartanhxdx=1. The Legendre polynomials are orthogonal and complete, and they expand the boundary values of an axisymmetric potential of a sphere.

  • Integer modes: a nonzero solution of Legendre’s equation bounded on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) exists exactly for λ=ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)λ=ℓ(ℓ+1), ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}ℓ∈{0,1,2,…}, and is a multiple of PℓP_\ellPℓ​.

  • Rodrigues: Pℓ=12ℓℓ! ⁣dℓ ⁣dxℓ(x2−1)ℓP_\ell=\frac1{2^\ell\ell!}\frac{\dd^\ell}{\dd x^\ell}(x^2-1)^\ellPℓ​=2ℓℓ!1​dxℓdℓ​(x2−1)ℓ, Pℓ(1)=1P_\ell(1)=1Pℓ​(1)=1, Pℓ(−x)=(−1)ℓPℓ(x)P_\ell(-x)=(-1)^\ell P_\ell(x)Pℓ​(−x)=(−1)ℓPℓ​(x), ∣Pℓ∣≤1\abs{P_\ell}\le1∣Pℓ​∣≤1 on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1].

  • Norms: ∫−11PℓPk ⁣dx=2δℓk/(2ℓ+1)\int_{-1}^1P_\ell P_k\dd x=2\delta_{\ell k}/(2\ell+1)∫−11​Pℓ​Pk​dx=2δℓk​/(2ℓ+1).

  • Completeness: for piecewise continuous fff, SNf→fS_Nf\to fSN​f→f in the mean square, with Parseval’s identity (40.8).

  • Sphere: u=∑ℓcℓ(r/a)ℓPℓ(cos⁡θ)u=\sum_\ell c_\ell(r/a)^\ell P_\ell(\cos\theta)u=∑ℓ​cℓ​(r/a)ℓPℓ​(cosθ) inside and ∑ℓcℓ(a/r)ℓ+1Pℓ(cos⁡θ)\sum_\ell c_\ell(a/r)^{\ell+1}P_\ell(\cos\theta)∑ℓ​cℓ​(a/r)ℓ+1Pℓ​(cosθ) outside, with cℓ=2ℓ+12∫−11fPℓ ⁣dxc_\ell=\frac{2\ell+1}2\int_{-1}^1fP_\ell\dd xcℓ​=22ℓ+1​∫−11​fPℓ​dx.
